caption:
Bankrupt Character.AI plans to auction its platform on December 1, including chat histories from more than 21 million US accounts.
More than 2.1 million of those accounts are registered to minors, and 42 state attorneys general have asked the court to reject the sale as written.
The lead bidder was formed one day before Character.AI picked it.

Should a bankrupt app be allowed to sell your private chats?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Gizmodo, Notebookcheck · Photo: Shutterstock, Getty Images

paragraphs.text: A coalition of 42 state attorneys general has asked a federal bankruptcy court to stop Character.AI from selling its platform and user data in its current form. The company, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2026, plans to hold an auction on December 1, 2026, according to Gizmodo and Notebookcheck.
The states filed their objection on November 24, 2026, Notebookcheck reported. Gizmodo reported that the objection was filed in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware.

The auction covers the Character.AI platform along with chat histories from more than 21 million US accounts, according to Notebookcheck. More than 2.1 million of those accounts are registered to minors. The attorneys general wrote in their filing that the data at stake is vast and sensitive, Gizmodo reported, and said that as of March 2025 the service had more than 21.6 million US users.

According to the states, the chats include conversations in which users disclosed confidential mental or medical health information, including in therapy-like exchanges. Notebookcheck reported that each chat is linked to a user profile, an IP address and risk scores that Character.AI assigned itself. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said IP addresses and other metadata are part of the sale.

Character.AI's website says the company does not sell personal information for monetary consideration and is not a data broker, Gizmodo noted. Since the bankruptcy began, the company has only said that user data continues to be protected under its privacy policy, according to Notebookcheck.

The lead bidder is Smirks & Pangs Acquisition LLC. The coalition pointed out that the company was formed in Delaware on November 13, 2026, one day before Character.AI selected it as the base bid. Gizmodo, citing The Wall Street Journal, reported that a bankruptcy judge approved the selection on November 24 after Character.AI disclosed that the bidder was backed by the New York investment firm Octave Advisors.

Under the proposed terms, the buyer would not have to follow Character.AI's privacy policy or honor opt-out and deletion requests, Notebookcheck reported, and could pass the data to another company without telling users, the states or the court. If Character.AI sells to a different bidder, Smirks & Pangs would collect a $350,000 break-up fee.

The states want the court to reject the sale in its current form. At a minimum, Bonta's office said, any sale must leave out children's chats and other sensitive data and include conditions that protect users. In a post on X, Bonta said bankruptcy should not be used to get around the law. The court has appointed a consumer privacy ombudsman to review how the data is handled, Notebookcheck reported.

Character.AI lets users chat with customizable AI companions, many based on celebrities or fictional characters. The company has faced lawsuits over the safety of young users, including a 2024 suit from a Florida mother over the death of her 14-year-old son, and a lawsuit from the Kentucky attorney general, Gizmodo reported. Disney separately offered $20 million for a nonexclusive license to the company's intellectual property, a deal that has not been approved in court and that would reportedly not include chats.

For users who want their data out before the sale, Notebookcheck reported that account deletion takes effect immediately, under Profile Settings, Account, Manage Account & Data on the web, or Remove Account in the app. A chat export takes three to four weeks, so a request made now would arrive after the auction. The company has not said whether a deletion made before the sale is guaranteed to take effect.

The case tests whether promises made in a privacy policy survive when the company that made them goes bankrupt. Chatbot companions collect far more personal material than most apps, because many people use them like a diary or a counselor, and the states are arguing that this material cannot simply be treated as an asset to be sold to the highest bidder.

The bankruptcy court's ruling on the objection, expected before or around the December 1 auction, will decide whether chats from millions of users, including minors, can change hands and under what conditions.
